hook: The missing planes were the data.

instagram.caption:
The missing planes were the data.

1943. Bombers came home riddled with holes — wings, tails, fuselage. Almost nothing on the engines. The Air Force wanted armor where the bullets landed. Abraham Wald, a statistician at Columbia, said that was the wrong question.

The returning planes showed where a hit could be survived. The untouched engines marked where planes didn't come back from. Armor there.

It hides in every five-star review, every winning stock chart, every list of who made it.

alt_text: A vertical short-form video. Title card reads 'The planes that didn't come back.' Three cinematic images follow: a rain-slick wartime airfield with a battered bomber, bullet holes peppered across its wings and tail and its engines dark and intact; a mathematician's cluttered desk under a single brass lamp, a faceless figure bent over an annotated fuselage diagram with red-ink bullet clusters and blank untouched areas near the engines; a hand at a kitchen counter scrolling a wall of five-star reviews on a phone, a stock chart visible behind it. A formula card builds the Bayes' theorem equation P(S given H_R) step by step. Axi the mascot reads at the top of each card.
